name: Rust
vendor: Rust Project, supported by the Rust Foundation
summary: A systems language that frees memory without a garbage collector, because the compiler checks ownership and borrowing rules before the program runs.
intro: Rust compiles to machine code, with no garbage collector and no heavy runtime, so its libraries can stand in for C. Memory safety comes from three ownership rules the compiler enforces: each value has one owner, there is only one owner at a time, and the value is dropped (freed) when its owner goes out of scope. Code can borrow a value through references instead of taking it, but at any moment there may be either one mutable reference or any number of immutable ones. The borrow checker applies these rules at compile time, with no cost at run time, and the same rules rule out data races between threads. Code that needs to break them, to call C or touch raw pointers, goes in an `unsafe` block, which unlocks exactly five extra operations and marks where to look when something goes wrong.

A new stable compiler ships every six weeks, and Rust 1.0 (May 2015) began a promise that stable code keeps compiling. Changes that would break old code, such as new keywords, go into editions instead: 2015, 2018, 2021 and 2024, the last stabilized with Rust 1.85 in February 2025. Each crate picks its edition in `Cargo.toml`, crates of different editions link together freely, and Cargo’s migration tooling rewrites most code automatically. Cargo, the bundled build tool and package manager, pulls dependencies from crates.io.
strengths: Memory safety and freedom from data races without a garbage collector, checked by the compiler rather than discovered in production
Low-level control with no garbage collector or runtime, so a Rust library can be a drop-in replacement for one written in C
Cargo, the bundled build tool and package manager, crates.io and `rustfmt` make dependencies and code style consistent across the ecosystem
Editions let the language change without splitting the ecosystem: old and new crates link together
limits: Slow compilation tops the list of productivity complaints in the project’s own 2024 user survey
The borrow checker is deliberately conservative: it rejects some valid programs, so some designs need restructuring or `unsafe` to compile
Async Rust is a frequent source of struggle in survey answers, and users worry the language is growing too complex
`unsafe` blocks and C libraries reached through FFI are not checked by the compiler, so safety rests on reviewing them

story: In 2006 Graydon Hoare, a programmer at Mozilla, came home to find the elevator in his Vancouver building broken again, its software crashed. Many such crashes come from memory bugs in C and C++. Hoare started Rust as a side project to get the speed of those languages without their memory errors.

Mozilla saw that Rust could help it build a safer browser engine and began sponsoring it officially in 2009, paying a team of engineers that included Patrick Walton, Niko Matsakis and Felix Klock. They built the ownership system that lets the compiler prove memory is used safely. Hoare stepped back in 2013. Rust 1.0 came out on 15 May 2015, ending years of breaking changes, and Mozilla used the language for its Servo engine and for the CSS engine in Firefox.

In February 2021 Mozilla handed Rust’s trademarks and infrastructure, including the crates.io registry, to the new Rust Foundation, a non-profit founded with AWS, Huawei, Google, Microsoft and Mozilla. The project itself stays independent and run by its own teams.

choices.choice: Ownership checked at compile time instead of a garbage collector
choices.why: Rust wanted C’s control and speed for code like browser engines. Tracking who owns each value lets the compiler insert the frees itself, so there is no collector and no pause, yet no use-after-free or double free.

choices.choice: One mutable reference or many readers, never both
choices.why: The same rule that prevents dangling pointers also rules out data races, which is what the Rust team called “fearless concurrency”: threads can share data only in ways the compiler can check.

choices.choice: Stability without stagnation: six-week releases and editions
choices.why: After 1.0, breaking changes were mostly out of scope. Releases follow a train model like Firefox and Chrome, and changes that would break code, such as the `async` keyword, wait for an opt-in edition.
Some code, such as calling C or writing low-level data structures, can’t be checked. Rust allows it inside marked blocks, so the unchecked parts are small and easy to find.

timeline.text: Graydon Hoare starts Rust as a personal project
Rust 1.0 released on 15 May; releases every six weeks after that
Rust 2018, the first new edition, ships with Rust 1.31
Rust Foundation founded in February; Rust 2021 edition in 1.56
Rust 2024 edition stable with Rust 1.85 in February
